body:
Why public-health programmes are needed

Many health problems cannot be prevented through treatment of individual patients alone. Immunisation, infectious-disease surveillance, sanitation, reproductive-health services and screening for chronic diseases require organised action across communities.

India's health programmes address different needs. Some primarily prevent infection; others organise early detection, maternal and child care, adolescent health or long-term disease management.

Important national programmes

ProgrammeImportant date or scopeMain purpose
Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)Named UIP in 1985; earlier Expanded Programme on Immunization began in 1978Routine vaccination against specified vaccine-preventable diseases
Mission IndradhanushLaunched in December 2014Improve immunisation coverage among unvaccinated and partially vaccinated children
Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK)Launched on 7 January 2014; adolescents aged 10–19Adolescent health, including nutrition, sexual and reproductive health, mental health and substance-use prevention
RMNCAH+N approachIntroduced in 2013Continuum of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and nutrition services
National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)RNTCP renamed NTEP in 2020TB detection, treatment, prevention and patient support
National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme (NVBDCP)Implemented through the national vector-borne disease-control systemPrevention and control of malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis, kala-azar and lymphatic filariasis
National Programme for Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases (NP-NCD)Current programme name; includes population-based screening of adults aged 30 years and abovePrevention, screening, management and referral for major NCDs

Routine immunisation and Mission Indradhanush

The Universal Immunization Programme is the continuing system for providing specified vaccines through public health services. It includes vaccines against important childhood infections, according to the applicable national immunisation schedule.

Mission Indradhanush is a targeted effort to reach children who missed routine vaccination or did not receive all recommended doses. Its purpose is to improve coverage, particularly in underserved or difficult-to-reach areas.

UIP provides routine immunisation services. Mission Indradhanush strengthens efforts to reach people who have missed those services. It does not replace the routine immunisation programme.

Adolescent and reproductive-health services

Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram addresses health concerns of adolescents aged 10–19 years. Its scope is broader than reproductive health alone. It includes nutrition, mental health, prevention of substance misuse, prevention of injuries and violence, and access to suitable counselling and healthcare.

The RMNCAH+N approach recognises that the health of women and children is connected across life stages. Health and nutrition during adolescence can influence later reproductive health. Antenatal and childbirth services affect maternal and newborn outcomes, while postnatal services support recovery and child development.

Communicable-disease programmes

The National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme focuses on early detection of TB, appropriate treatment, prevention of transmission and support for affected people. Its name expresses an elimination objective; it does not mean that tuberculosis has already disappeared from India.

The National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC) is the central agency associated with the National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme. The programme addresses 6 major vector-borne diseases: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis, kala-azar and lymphatic filariasis.

Vector-borne disease control requires community participation. Detecting cases is important, but so are mosquito-source reduction, personal protection and measures suited to local transmission patterns.

Noncommunicable-disease prevention

NP-NCD provides a public-health framework for prevention and control of major noncommunicable diseases. Population-based screening includes adults aged 30 years and above and focuses on conditions such as hypertension, diabetes and common cancers, including oral, breast and cervical cancers.

Screening is followed by appropriate assessment and referral when needed. It does not mean that every person screened has a disease.

Gujarat connection: e-Mamta and Mamta Divas

Gujarat's e-Mamta initiative was introduced as a name-based mother-and-child tracking system through collaboration involving the state health department and the National Informatics Centre. It was designed to register pregnant women, children and adolescents and track services such as antenatal care, postnatal care, immunisation and nutrition.

The key public-health concept behind such a system is continuity of care. Tracking helps identify individuals who may have missed a service and need follow-up. The initiative is an example of health-information management, rather than a clinical test or treatment.

Mamta Divas, described in Gujarat municipal health services as a health and nutrition activity, brings preventive and maternal-child health services closer to communities. Activities include registration for antenatal and postnatal care, health check-ups, vaccination, growth monitoring, supplementation and counselling.

These services demonstrate the role of Anganwadi centres, community health workers and urban health facilities in preventive healthcare. The same community contact can connect families to further clinical services when necessary.

Understanding programme dates and status

Programme names, administrative arrangements and implementation phases can change. The programme descriptions above reflect official information consulted up to 3 November 2026. The listed years are programme-history facts, not claims about the results achieved in 2026.

In particular, the NTEP's elimination objective should be distinguished from actual achievement of elimination. Similarly, information about the historical introduction of e-Mamta should not be interpreted as a claim about its precise current software coverage or operational performance.

Prelims focus

  • The Expanded Programme on Immunization began in 1978 and was renamed UIP in 1985.
  • Mission Indradhanush was launched in December 2014.
  • RKSK was launched on 7 January 2014 and covers adolescents aged 10–19.
  • NTEP is the national programme focused on tuberculosis elimination.
  • NP-NCD includes population-based screening for adults aged 30 years and above.
  • Gujarat's e-Mamta is a mother-and-child service-tracking initiative.
  • Trap: The existence of a disease-elimination target does not prove that the disease has been eliminated.

title: India and Gujarat: Essential Public-Health Programmes and Their Functions
